frames.narration: Both pipelines resolve the popular package httputil, three levels down your 400-dependency tree, to 1.2.3. Build A uses the range ^1.2.0 with no lockfile. Build B has a lockfile that records 1.2.3 and its SHA-256.

Day 10: the attacker takes over the maintainer's account (a phished login without 2FA) and publishes httputil 1.2.9 with a postinstall script that sends environment variables away. It is a normal, correctly signed-in publish.
The vulnerability scanner checks the advisory database and finds nothing. No CVE exists for a release nobody has reported, so a scan can only say 'no known problems'.
Build A runs every day. The range ^1.2.0 allows 1.2.9, so it installs it and runs the postinstall script on the CI runner. Days 10 to 14 add up to 44 builds that pulled the bad version.
Build B installs from its lockfile: still 1.2.3, and the hash matches. The lockfile keeps the build identical, but it only holds until someone updates it.

Day 14: the weekly update bot runs inside the attack window and opens a PR bumping httputil to 1.2.9. CI is green, it auto-merges, and the new hash is recorded. A hash of the bad file does not make the file good.

Day 15: a researcher reports it. The registry yanks 1.2.9 and publishes an advisory, so the scanner now flags it. Build A is clean from the next run, but Build B keeps 1.2.9 in its lockfile until a fix lands on day 17: 22 builds in total.

The trade-off. A 6-day minimum release age would have refused 1.2.9 (eligible day 16, yanked day 15), so 0 builds. But the real CVE fix published on day 12 would also have waited: 6 days late floating, 9 days with the weekly bot.
